title: Refactoring State: mv, rm, and import
intro: Code changes, but infrastructure shouldn't be destroyed just because you renamed something. These commands change what Terraform thinks it manages without touching the real resources.

steps.prompt: You renamed resource 'aws_instance.web' to 'aws_instance.frontend' in the code. Tell Terraform it's the same resource, just moved to a new address.
steps.explanation: The real server is untouched — only its address in state changes.
steps.why: Without this, plan sees 'web' removed from code (destroy!) and 'frontend' added (create!) — replacing a production server just because of a rename. Modern Terraform (1.1+) also supports a 'moved {}' block in code, which does the same thing but gets reviewed in a pull request — preferable for teams.

steps.prompt: Confirm the rename produced no real changes.
steps.fake_output: No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.
steps.explanation: The server is now tracked under its new name, with nothing to create or destroy.
steps.why: Always plan immediately after state surgery. If plan wants to destroy anything, the mv didn't do what you expected — stop and investigate before any apply.

steps.prompt: An old S3 bucket, 'legacy-logs', should no longer be managed by Terraform, but must NOT be deleted. Remove it from state only.
steps.fake_output:
Removed aws_s3_bucket.legacy_logs
Successfully removed 1 resource instance(s).
steps.explanation: Terraform forgets the bucket exists; the bucket and its data stay in AWS.
steps.why: Just deleting the resource block from code would make the next apply DESTROY the bucket. 'state rm' plus deleting the block from code is how you hand a resource off to be managed some other way, safely.

steps.prompt: A security group, sg-0a1b2c3d4e, was created manually in the console. You've written a matching 'aws_security_group.admin' block — now bring the real one under Terraform's management.
steps.fake_output:
aws_security_group.admin: Importing from ID "sg-0a1b2c3d4e"...
Import successful!

The resources that were imported are shown above. These resources are now in your Terraform state and will henceforth be managed by Terraform.
steps.explanation: The existing resource is recorded in state under your address, without being recreated.
steps.why: Import only writes state — it doesn't write your .tf code. That's why the next step matters. Terraform 1.5+ also offers 'import {}' blocks and 'plan -generate-config-out' to draft the code for you.

steps.prompt: Check whether your hand-written code actually matches the imported resource.
steps.fake_output:
# aws_security_group.admin will be updated in-place
  ~ description = "Managed by Terraform" -> "Admin access"
Plan: 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy.
steps.explanation: One mismatch: your code's description differs from the real one.
steps.why: The goal after an import is a clean plan. Adjust your code to match reality (here, set description = "Admin access") rather than letting apply 'correct' a live resource you only just started managing — some changes, like a security group description, force full replacement.
